[MUQATIL:19:41-44/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Ibrahim asks his father Azar why he worships idols that cannot hear or see and cannot benefit him in the Hereafter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A deficient noun has a final weak radical after a short vowel; its final alif replaces yāʾ or wāw, which do not show ordinary case endings.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some short nouns such as قفا, رحى, and رجا البئر cannot be identified as deficient by analogy alone; hearing establishes their weak origin.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An extended noun has final yāʾ or wāw after an alif; analogy with sound-root forms can identify it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbal nouns from patterns such as استسقى, اشترى, and أعطى are extended because their final weak radical follows an alif, as in regular-root analogues.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as الاحبنطاء and الاسلنقاء are extended by the same pattern: the weak radical would follow an alif if replaced by a sound consonant.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sound-related verbal nouns with initial ḍamma, such as العواء, الدعاء, and الزقاء, indicate an extended weak-root form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl says speakers who shorten البكاء make it parallel to الحزن.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Action nouns such as النزاء follow the extended pattern, comparable to the regular-root القناص.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A verbal noun with initial ḍamma is rarely deficient because the corresponding فعل pattern is seldom a verbal noun outside weak-root forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some extended forms are recognizable only by hearing, including السماء, الرشاء, الآلاء, and المقلاء.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A plural on أفعلة normally points to an extended singular, as with أقبية and أرشية; ندى وأندية is an exception.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as معطى and مشترى are identified as deficient by comparison with regular patterns such as مخرج and معترك.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Group nouns whose singular is on فعلة or فعلة are short, as in عروة/عرى and فرية/فرى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The forms مسلقى and مسلنقى follow سليقيته: a corresponding sound consonant would occur after a short vowel, revealing the weak radical.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the sound-root counterpart is an adjective on أفعل with a verbal noun on فعل, weak-root forms such as أعشى, أعمى, and أقنى are deficient.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If a verb is فعل يفعل and its noun is فعل, its weak-root verbal noun is deficient; examples include هوى, ردى, صدى, لوى, كرى, and غوى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same inference applies when فعل يفعل has a sound-root noun on فعلان, as in عطشان and ظمآن; weak-root examples include طوى and صدى.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | غرى has the anomalously extended form الغراء, compared also with الظماء; such exceptions are learned from usage.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | رضا also departs from its regular comparison with سخط; its vowel pattern cannot be generalized without attested usage.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالمقصوروالممدود)#648/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The form بدا is likewise accepted from attestation, with حلب offered as its sound-root parallel; such forms cannot confidently be produced without hearing them.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p226/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | Abraham's father worshipped idols that neither hear nor see nor benefit anyone.
[TAB-FULL:v15p549#2/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | An idol cannot answer when called, see or assist its worshipper, or remove harm, unlike the Lord who can do these things.
[TAB-FULL:v15p549#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويو البصرة | reports | Basran grammarians treat the h in أبت as an added vocative form; in pause it is abah, while connected or possessive forms use the t, and they allow the shortened vocative ab. | mentions 12:4
[TAB-FULL:v15p549#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويو الكوفة | reports | Kufan grammarians say the h in abah/ummah is a pause marker that became common; when a possessive yā is sought, it is pronounced t in يا أبت.
[TAB-FULL:v15p549#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · نحويو الكوفة | reports | With the lamentation alif, يا أبتا can pause with t or h; pausing in h is unusual except under an analysis like the cited shortened Arabic form.
[TAB-FULL:v15p549/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī introduces Abraham, God's intimate friend, and recounts that he was truthful in speech, reports, and promises. | mentions 3:41
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | In address the Arabs say يا أبة and يا أمة, but do not use أبتي or أمتي in ordinary reported speech; the pause form is يا أبه.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh compare يا أبة to vocatives such as يا عمة and يا خالة; the form can address a male or female.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The dual أبوان shows that the mother shares in the term of parenthood; the cited Qur'anic wording is “his parents inherited him.” | mentions 4:11
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The form also parallels feminine-looking descriptors used for males, such as رجل ربعة and غلام يفعة.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · الخليل | reports | The hāʾ in أبة replaces the possessive yāʾ of يا أبي or يا أمي; it occurs only in address because yāʾ is often dropped there.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Possessive yāʾ may be omitted in vocative يا أب, but not in non-vocative قال أب when “my father” is intended.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p331/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Feminine forms can describe males, as in امرأة طالق وطاهر; نفس is feminine even when three persons are called ثلاثة أنفس.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p332/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The objects that neither hear, see, nor benefit are idols.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p48/r1] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu Amr compares his generation with earlier scholars to small plants at the roots of tall palms, expressing their lesser stature.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p48/r2] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Ibn Mujahid compares transmission criticism in readings with hadith criticism: reports may be accepted and widespread, rejected despite transmission, or corrected as mistakes by specialists.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p48/r3] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | He classifies reading reports as sound and widespread, sound but uncommon, rare dialect, weak in grammar though recited, obvious error, or subtle error discerned only by expert grammarians.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p48/r4] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | Only specialists in reports and legal rulings can properly evaluate disputed transmissions; persistence in an error may discredit a transmitter.
[IBNMUJAHID:v1p48/r5] IBNMUJAHID, d. 324 · author | holds | The regional readings of Mecca, Medina, Kufa, Basra, and Syria were received from predecessors and followed a locally established reader whose reading was accepted publicly and privately.
[NAHHAS:v3p18/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | The pause on يا أبت may use hāʾ because it is a feminine ending; Ibn Kaysān permits stopping on tāʾ because it attaches to an inseparable element.
[NAHHAS:v3p18/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī says عصي and عاصي have the same meaning.
[SULAMI:v1p427/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Do not rely on one who cannot hear your prayer, see your state, or meet any of your needs.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p242/r1] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The deity must possess hearing and sight perfectly, without deficiency; the same standard applies to power over benefit and harm.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p242/r2] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | No created being can originate or create; attaching the heart to a creature or imagining even a sliver of independent efficacy resembles idol worship.
[QUSHAYRI:v2p242/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | Abraham showed every form of compassion, but repeated counsel did not help his father because later effort cannot undo a prior decree of exclusion.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v14p253#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The vocative ending in يا أبت was discussed at the start of Joseph; Abraham rebukes his father for worshipping an idol without hearing or sight that can avert harm or help. | mentions 12:4
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:19:40-42/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Abraham asks why his father worships what cannot hear prayer, see worship, or protect him from God's punishment.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p326/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Figurative action can lie in the act itself: someone escaping near-death is said to have been created anew because the near-death state is treated as nonexistence.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p326/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | By contrast, saying spring made flowers uses a real act of making but figuratively attributes it to spring rather than to God, the true agent.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p326/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In the Quranic phrase about reviving earth after its death, Jurjani says the metaphor lies in 'lif

e' itself, since the intended referent is other than the earth, not in attributing the act. | mentions 30:19
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p326/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A thing cannot be called metaphorical or literal merely as something asserted: every assertion must belong to something, so those labels concern the content asserted or its attribution.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p326/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Derived verbs such as weaving, forging, embroidering, and painting name real processes; saying spring performs them is figurative in attributing the action, not in the action word.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p326/r6] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In 'the report pleased me,' pleasure is real, so the metaphor is the attribution that makes the report seem to cause it; this cannot be a lexical metaphor in the verb.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p60/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Calling one person 'the man' can elevate him so completely that everyone else is excluded from the category; the wording treats their existence as absence.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p60/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A milder 'this is a man' can mean someone of full stature without denying that other people are men; 'this is something' can likewise mean merely countable or especially significant.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p60/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | When opposed qualities differ in excellence, lack of the superior quality may be named by its opposite: life without knowledge is death, and unbeneficial sight or hearing is called blindness or deafness.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p60/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Calling someone deaf and blind in this usage means he gains nothing from what he hears or sees, as if he had neither faculty.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p60/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In a qualified expression such as 'deaf to what offends, hearing otherwise,' both qualities coexist generally; deafness is limited to a class or circumstance, not asserted absolutely.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p128/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | An object may be absent because the point is to assert the act itself as characteristic, without specifying something the act affects.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p128/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Saying he gives dinars specifies what he gives; it does not merely assert that he gives, so adding an object changes the focus.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p128/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A second kind has a definite object understood from context: the conventional examples mean one lends an ear and lowers an eyelid.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p128/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Artful omission hides a specific known object so the speaker seems to assert the action alone, producing an additional rhetorical effect.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p128/r5] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Buḥturī’s line implicitly says that observers see al-Muʿtazz’s virtues and listeners hear their report; the omitted objects let the poet conceal the intended praise.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p128/r6] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The poem praises al-Muʿtazz while alluding to al-Mustaʿīn: visible and audible virtues prove the former’s right to the caliphate and torment rivals who know it.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Some compositions require the parts to be planned together, with meanings interwoven and later clauses strongly bound to earlier ones; their forms are varied rather than governed by one exhaustive rule.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r10] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | An unnamed poet first contrasts the listener’s hoped-for permanence with his own, then concludes that tomorrow will bring a change from both states.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r11] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The ending جمع فيما قسم by saying both parties will experience a change tomorrow; its effect is heightened by the preceding statement that this thought brought peace.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | One form pairs meanings across condition and result; al-Buḥturī’s paired love and estrangement clauses show the structure.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Another paired conditional makes a remembered kinship bring tears just as conflict brings bloodshed.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Quḍāʿī juxtaposes falling from high rank with a renewed rise, then prosperity with hardship followed by wealth.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r5] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Kathīr compares his pursuit of ʿAzza to seeking shade that disappears, while al-Buḥturī depicts time’s force against the weak as the strong’s attack.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r6] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The second half of Kathīr’s comparison completes the image of the cloud’s vanishing shade as the seeker settles beneath it.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r7] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Al-Buḥturī’s oath introduces an image of time’s aggression against the weak by the powerful, another tightly paired construction.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r8] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Division followed by collection is especially elegant: Ḥassān first separates harm to enemies from benefit to allies, then gathers these traits under one inherited disposition.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p87/r9] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | Ḥassān’s next line gathers the divided traits into a single disposition, strengthened by the statement that new traits are the worst.
[DAMGHANI:v1p13#2/r3] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Ab can mean one’s actual father, as in Abraham’s address to his father and the references to Āzar and parents. | mentions 6:74, 80:34
[JISHUMI:v6p4562/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · ابن عامر وأبو جعفر | reports | These readers use fatḥa on the tāʾ in يا أبت throughout the Qur'an; the others use kasra.
[JISHUMI:v6p4562/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Abraham addresses his father Āzar, who was an unbeliever.
[JISHUMI:v6p4562/r15] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Worship may mean worship, supplication, submission, or obedience; the objects may be idols or all celestial bodies and other things his people worshipped.
[JISHUMI:v6p4562/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The tāʾ intensifies the possessive address; kasra seeks the possessive yāʾ and the stop retains tāʾ.
[JISHUMI:v6p4562/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj permits stopping with hāʾ.
[JISHUMI:v6p4562/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · غير مسمى | reports | Another analysis makes tāʾ replace the possessive yāʾ; fatḥa can represent يا أبتاه.
[JISHUMI:v6p4564/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Only a benefactor possessing original blessings—God, powerful, knowing, living, eternal—deserves worship; idols lack these attributes.
[JISHUMI:v6p4566/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Abraham's father was an unbeliever, as other Qur'anic verses say, so the plain meaning should not be displaced by figurative reinterpretation.
[JISHUMI:v6p4566/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Worship and following are acts of human agents, contradicting the opponents' doctrine about created acts.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p234/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Abraham's father is identified as Azar, who worshipped idols.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p234/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Abraham says idols cannot hear sounds, see anything, or provide any benefit or sufficiency.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · الرسول صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم | reports | A prophetic report says God told Abraham, His close friend, to perfect his manners even toward unbelievers, promising him shelter beneath the Throne and nearness to God.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r12] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Each of Abraham's four counsels begins yā-abati as a plea for closeness and compassion.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r13] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | In mā lā yasmaʿ and mā lam ya'tika, mā may be relative or descriptive; the object of 'hears' and 'sees' is omitted and not intended.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r14] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Shayʾan can be an accusative verbal noun meaning any benefit, with a parallel sense supplied for the preceding verbs.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r15] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Alternatively, shayʾan is a direct object, following the expression aghna ʿannī wajhak.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Abraham first asks why his father worships, to awaken him to the grave persistence and excess of his error.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Even a living, discerning, hearing, seeing, powerful created being is not fit for worship or lordship, even if an angel or prophet.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship is the highest veneration and belongs only to the ultimate benefactor, creator, provider, life-giver, death-giver, rewarder, and punisher.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r5] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Worship directed elsewhere is injustice, defiance, error, disbelief, and departure from clear truth.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v3p21/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | An inert idol plainly cannot hear praise, see worship, avert harm, or meet a need.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p17#3/r6] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh treats the tāʾ in yā abati as replacing the possessive yāʾ and pauses on it as hāʾ; al-Farraʾ says the possessive yāʾ remains implicit and pause retains tāʾ.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p17#3/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Most readers kasra the tāʾ; Ibn Masud's codex has wāw for the vocative, and Ibn Amir, al-Aʿraj, and Abu Jaʿfar read fatḥa as if deleting the alif of yā abātā.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p17#3/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · هارون | reports | Harun faulted the fatḥa reading, th

ough another explanation treats the tāʾ as an inserted vocative marker like that in yā Ṭalḥa.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p18/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The object that neither hears nor sees is an idol; even perceptive beings such as angels would not thereby become worthy of worship, but the wording exposes idolatry's absurdity.
[TABRISI:19:41-44/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The father is Āzar; idols cannot hear prayer, see worshippers, or help them in worldly matters.
[TABRISI:19:41-44/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The tāʾ in yā abat intensifies possession; Ibrahim asks why his father worships what cannot benefit or harm him.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p111/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | With a light bāʾ, ab means father; with a doubled bāʾ, it means pasture, as in fākihatan wa-abbā.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p111/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The verb abba means to prepare to depart, with the forms abā, abābah, and abīban; al-Aʿshā supplies a poetic example.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p111/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | The first Qur’anic sense is a near or direct father, illustrated by Abraham addressing his father and other family passages. | mentions 4:11, 6:74, 28:23, 80:34
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p236#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | What the idols cannot avail against is harm: they cannot ward it off from you.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p62#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | rejects | Some say one may invoke God without mastering the premises; Razi rejects this as weak, since Abraham condemned worship of one who neither hears nor sees, and an incapable deity would fall under that criticism.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p62#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi uses Abraham's rebuke of his father in 19:42 to argue that God must be known as all-hearing, all-seeing, and powerful over all things.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p62#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A servant must know he cannot fully guard his interests: even knowing what is needed, he cannot acquire what is absent or preserve what is present unaided.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p62#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Certainty about these truths produces humility and brokenness, then inward petition and the spoken invocation for refuge.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p62#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | People are powerless in both knowledge and action, the two things issuing from them; Razi begins by demonstrating their dependence on God for knowledge.
